candidates.attacker_control: A remote STOMP client controls the frame headers sent to the application. `SimpMessageHeaderAccessor.getFirstNativeHeader("selector", headers)` (line 144) returns the raw client-supplied native header from a SUBSCRIBE frame, and that string is passed directly to `expressionParser.parseExpression(selector)` (line 147). The attacker also controls when a message is routed to the destination (e.g., by sending a SEND/MESSAGE frame), which triggers evaluation of the malicious expression for the malicious subscription.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked for restrictions on selector expressions: none exist in this snapshot (no SimpleEvaluationContext anywhere in the tree; no selector allow-list, no SpelParserConfiguration restriction). Checked that the selector header really is attacker-supplied native header (SimpMessageHeaderAccessor.getFirstNativeHeader). Checked that evaluation is reachable on ordinary message routing (not only on subscription). Checked that the parse/eval exception handling does not prevent execution (side effects happen inside getValue before/despite exceptions). Also verified the similarly famous static-resource traversal is not the live issue here: ResourceHttpRequestHandler.getResource has the `%`-decode re-check (lines 413-426) and PathResourceResolver.isResourceUnderLocation has the decoded `../` check (lines 193-201), which mitigate CVE-2016-9878-style `%2e%2e%2f` requests in this snapshot.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary code execution in the application JVM (Spring EL can access types and invoke methods via StandardEvaluationContext), e.g., invoking java.lang.Runtime/ProcessBuilder style payloads; at minimum, expression evaluation gives broad information disclosure and server-side side effects. This is a remote, unauthenticated-at-framework-level compromise of any WebSocket/STOMP simple-broker endpoint that permits subscriptions.
candidates.prerequisites: Application exposes a STOMP endpoint (typically STOMP over WebSocket) backed by the simple broker (SimpleBrokerMessageHandler, which by default creates a DefaultSubscriptionRegistry — lines 80-81) or any broker using DefaultSubscriptionRegistry; the default selector header name remains "selector"; the attacker can establish a session and subscribe/send (authentication may or may not be required; the issue is a broken authorization/input-trust boundary, not only an auth bypass).
candidates.root_cause: DefaultSubscriptionRegistry treats the client-controlled STOMP native header `selector` as a Spring EL expression: addSubscriptionInternal() parses it with a default SpelExpressionParser (line 147, expressionParser field line 76) and filterSubscriptions() later evaluates it with `new StandardEvaluationContext(message)` (line 212) and `expression.getValue(context, boolean.class)` (line 216). StandardEvaluationContext uses the default SpEL type locator/method resolvers, so expressions can reference types such as java.lang.Runtime and invoke static methods/constructors. There is no allow-list, no SimpleEvaluationContext, and no sanitization of the selector text; only parse/evaluation exceptions are caught and logged.
candidates.title: Remote SpEL injection via STOMP subscription `selector` header in DefaultSubscriptionRegistry
candidates.trace: STOMP SUBSCRIBE frame -> StompSubProtocolHandler/StompDecoder exposes native headers -> SimpleBrokerMessageHandler.handleMessageInternal SUBSCRIBE branch calls subscriptionRegistry.registerSubscription (lines 280-283) -> AbstractSubscriptionRegistry.addSubscription -> DefaultSubscriptionRegistry.addSubscriptionInternal reads native header "selector" (line 144) and SpelExpressionParser.parseExpression(selector) (line 147) -> subscription stores the Expression. Later, a MESSAGE routed to that destination -> SimpleBrokerMessageHandler.sendMessageToSubscribers -> DefaultSubscriptionRegistry.findSubscriptionsInternal -> filterSubscriptions -> context = new StandardEvaluationContext(message) with SimpMessageHeaderPropertyAccessor (lines 211-214) -> expression.getValue(context, boolean.class) (line 216) executes the attacker's expression in the application JVM. Even if the boolean conversion subsequently fails, side effects of the expression (method/constructor invocation) occur before the conversion/exception handling.
candidates.unverified: No runtime reproduction or test execution was performed (code execution, tests, and scanners are out of scope for this review). Reachability depends on the application actually exposing a STOMP/WebSocket endpoint with the simple broker; message routing must trigger evaluation for the subscribed destination. I could not confirm whether this snapshot's case metadata targets this CVE or a different one, so this is a lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-917 Expression Language Injection (leading to CWE-94 Code Injection/RCE)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned main-source tree (3,885 files) read-only: all module main sources visible; no test sources are present in the snapshot. Focused review on trust boundaries and sinks: Spring MVC static resource handling (ResourceHttpRequestHandler, PathResourceResolver, resolvers/transformers), URL/path utilities (StringUtils.cleanPath, UrlPathHelper, UriComponentsBuilder, WebUtils), CORS handling (CorsConfiguration, DefaultCorsProcessor, CorsFilter, handler mapping integration), XML/XXE defaults (SourceHttpMessageConverter, Jaxb2RootElementHttpMessageConverter, AbstractMarshaller), message-converter RFD protection, Spring EL usage (DefaultSubscriptionRegistry, bean/cache evaluators), remoting/deserialization (HttpInvoker, RMI object streams), WebSocket/STOMP origin checks and broker flow, and miscellaneous path/URL helper code. The single strongest source-evidenced candidate is the STOMP selector SpEL injection; other areas are listed as rejected/unconfirmed leads.
limitations: Only the exposed main sources are available; test sources, build/test harnesses, and case metadata (CVE/fix commit) are not present, so the association between this snapshot and a specific dataset case/CVE could not be confirmed.

No code was executed; no runtime reproduction, deployment configuration, or dependency analysis was performed. Reachability statements are based on source reading only and are marked as prerequisites/unverified.

Coverage is broad but not exhaustive: 3,885 files include many modules; I did not line-by-line audit every file (e.g., large areas of spring-beans lifecycle code, spring-orm/Hibernate integration, spring-jdbc metadata, spring-test mocks), so additional issues may exist there.

Because at most one candidate may be submitted, other plausible but weaker leads (Windows `..\` traversal gap, WebUtils scheme omission, HttpInvoker deserialization) are recorded only as rejected/unconfirmed leads.

rejected_leads.lead: CVE-2016-9878-style directory traversal in static resource handling (ResourceHttpRequestHandler/PathResourceResolver)
rejected_leads.reason: The 4.3.5-dev snapshot already contains the URLDecoder re-checks that reject decoded `..` sequences (ResourceHttpRequestHandler.getResource lines 413-426; PathResourceResolver.isResourceUnderLocation lines 193-201), so the classic encoded traversal PoC is mitigated; a claim of exploitability would contradict the present hardening.

rejected_leads.lead: Windows-only encoded-backslash traversal in PathResourceResolver.isResourceUnderLocation (only checks decoded `../`, not `..\`)
rejected_leads.reason: isResourceUnderLocation decodes resourcePath but only tests `contains("../")`; the `..\` variant is not rejected. Kept as unconfirmed because the attacker must get a literal backslash past the earlier ResourceHttpRequestHandler checks and the resource must actually resolve on a Windows-style filesystem/container; I could not verify a working path to the filesystem from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: WebUtils.isSameOrigin omits scheme comparison (host+port only, WebUtils lines 820-841)
rejected_leads.reason: The code and its own comment mention scheme but only compare host and port. This is a genuine hardening gap, but impact is narrow (cross-scheme same-host origins with matching ports) and attacker control over the alternate scheme/host is limited; weaker evidence and impact than the SpEL injection.

rejected_leads.lead: HttpInvoker Java deserialization of untrusted request bodies (RemoteInvocationSerializingExporter/HttpInvokerServiceExporter, CVE-2016-1000027 pattern)
rejected_leads.reason: Real unsafe-deserialization surface, but exploitation requires an application to deliberately expose an HTTP invoker endpoint, is a known 'intended usage / won't fix by design' issue with an explicit javadoc warning in the snapshot, and no fix commit/tests are associated; lower-quality candidate than the SpEL RCE.

rejected_leads.lead: Malformed Javadoc at CorsConfiguration.java lines 105-111 containing two stray code lines resembling a removed single-argument combine helper
rejected_leads.reason: Looks like an editing/packaging artifact, but the surrounding methods (checkOrigin, checkHttpMethod, checkHeaders, combine, applyPermitDefaultValues) match expected Spring 4.3 semantics on inspection; no exploitable behavior change could be demonstrated, so it was not submitted as a vulnerability.

summary: Snapshot is Spring Framework 4.3.5.BUILD-SNAPSHOT (~Dec 2016, main sources only, tests absent). I traced the strongest distinct issue to the STOMP simple-broker subscription registry, where a client-supplied native `selector` header is parsed as a Spring EL expression and evaluated with an unrestricted StandardEvaluationContext (`DefaultSubscriptionRegistry`). This matches the well-known CVE-2018-1270 pattern (remote SpEL/code execution via crafted selectors) and gives a remote code-execution impact with clear attacker control. The classic CVE-2016-9878 static-resource traversal is mitigated here (both URLDecoder ".." checks are present in ResourceHttpRequestHandler.getResource and PathResourceResolver.isResourceUnderLocation), so I did not submit that area as a candidate; a Windows-oriented gap without the `..\` check in PathResourceResolver and the missing scheme comparison in WebUtils.isSameOrigin were kept as lower-confidence rejected leads. Coverage is limited to main sources; tests, runtime validation, and deployment configuration were not available.
